t: System software and modes of processing
l: Hello and welcome to Digital Tech Revision, the podcast for CCEA GCSE Digital Technology. I'm Aoife.
And I'm Conor. Today's episode is lesson L06: System software and modes of processing.
So Conor, if someone only remembers one thing from today, what should it be?
Distinguish between system software and application software, and between packaged and tailored software. That is the heart of it.
Okay, take us through it properly.

Software is the set of instructions that tells the hardware what to do. It is split into two types. System software runs the computer itself. It acts as the link between the hardware and the programs the user wants to run. The most important piece of system software is the operating system, such as Windows, macOS, Android or iOS, which manages every other program.
Makes sense. Keep going.

Utility programs and device drivers are also system software. Application software lets the user carry out a particular task, such as writing an essay, editing a photo or browsing the web. Applications can be packaged (off-the-shelf), which means they are made for many users and are cheap and ready to use, or tailored (bespoke), which means they are written for one organisation. Tailored software fits the organisation's needs exactly, but it costs more and takes time to develop, because one customer pays for all the design, programming and testing.
Right. What else do we need to know?

The operating system shares out the computer's resources. First, it allocates memory. A program or file must be copied from storage into RAM before the processor can use it, so the OS finds free space in RAM, gives it to the program and keeps programs apart so they do not overwrite each other. When the program closes, the space is freed. Second, it allocates storage. The OS saves files on the storage drive, records where each one is, frees the space when files are deleted and controls who can open them.
Got it. Keep going.

Third, it allocates processing time. The processor can only do one thing at a time on each core, so the OS splits its time into tiny time slices and hands them to each task in turn. Tasks with a higher priority receive more slices. The switching is so quick that several programs appear to run at once. The OS also starts the computer: when it is switched on, instructions held in ROM check the hardware and load the operating system into RAM.
And is there anything people often mix up here?

In real-time processing, data is processed as soon as it is entered and the output is ready quickly enough to affect the next input. Booking systems need this. When someone buys a ticket for a concert, the seat must be marked as sold straight away, or another person could buy the same seat. Air traffic control is even more critical, because an aircraft's position on screen must always be up to date. In batch processing, data is collected over a period, such as a week or a month, and then processed in one go without people being involved.
Okay. Keep going.

It suits large amounts of similar data where an instant result is not needed. An electricity company keeps a master file of customer details. New meter readings go into a temporary transaction file. Overnight, each reading is matched to its customer using the account number, the bill is calculated, all the bills are produced together, and the master file is updated for next time.
Go on.

A multi-user system lets many people, each at a different computer or terminal, share the processor of one powerful computer at the same time. It is also called a time-sharing system. The operating system gives each user a very short time slice of processor time in turn. When it has served the last user it goes back to the first, which is known as the round robin method. Because the processor works so quickly, each person feels as if they have the whole computer to themselves.
Right. Keep going.

For example, if four users each get a 20-millisecond slice, every user gets a turn every 80 milliseconds, which is twelve and a half times every second. Multi-user is not the same as real-time. Real-time describes how quickly data is processed, while multi-user describes how one processor is shared between many people. A system can be both, such as an online booking system used by many customers at once.
Time for quickfire key terms. I'll say the term, and you give me the answer the mark scheme gives credit for.
Go for it.
System software?
Software that runs and manages the computer hardware and acts as the interface between the hardware and application programs, e dot g. the operating system, utilities and device drivers.
Application software?
Software designed to let the user carry out a specific task, such as word processing, spreadsheets or web browsing.
Operating system?
System software that manages the computer's resources, allocating memory, storage and processing time, and lets the hardware and application software work together.
Boot-up sequence?
The steps carried out when a computer is switched on: instructions in ROM check the hardware and load the operating system from storage into RAM.
Real-time processing?
Each input is processed the moment it is entered, so the output is produced in time to affect the next input, e dot g. ticket booking or air traffic control.
Batch processing?
Similar data is collected into batches over a period and processed together later, without human involvement, often overnight, e dot g. bills and payroll.
What about the exam? Where has this come up?

Questions on this lesson often use command words such as describe and distinguish, and they nearly always want an example. Real-time processing appeared in the 2022 paper, question 1 and was compared with multi-user processing in the 2023 paper, question 5. Strong answers said real-time processes each input immediately so the output affects the next input, and that multi-user shares one processor between many users using time slices. the 2023 paper, question 5 asked which resources the operating system manages: name memory, storage and processing time, and say what the OS does with each. Batch processing came up in the 2023 paper, question 12; mention collecting data over time, processing it together without human input, and a suitable example such as bills or payroll. In the 2025 paper, question 4 the Chief Examiner reported that many pupils could not describe the boot-up sequence, so learn the order: ROM instructions run, hardware is checked, the OS is loaded into RAM. Key-term matching also tested definitions from this lesson.

Let's finish with a question for the listeners. Which task is best suited to batch processing? Is it A, Booking a concert seat; B, Controlling traffic lights; C, Producing monthly electricity bills; D, Playing an online game?
I'll give you a few seconds.
The answer is C: Producing monthly electricity bills. Bills involve lots of similar data that can be collected and processed together later.
